title: Resume, Portfolio and Job Hunting
subtitle: Show the work, not the adjectives
summary: A free course on making what you can do visible to somebody who is skimming. Nine lessons on a resume that survives a fast first pass, a portfolio that shows finished work instead of claiming it, an application that is not the paragraph everyone else sent, and honest answers about a gap, a credential or a rate. Written for people applying to Philippine employers and to overseas remote roles, and the exam at the end issues a verifiable certificate.
description: Being right for the job is not what gets you read. Somewhere between your inbox and a shortlist there is a person moving fast through a pile, looking for a reason to keep you in, and your application either gives them one in the first few lines or it does not. This course is about that moment and everything that has to be true before it. You build an evidence inventory of work you have actually finished, turn it into a one page resume ordered for a skimmer, assemble a small portfolio with a case note under each piece, and write applications that prove you read the ad. Then the parts people avoid: what to say about a gap, how to state a credential so it means something, how to answer the expected pay question for a local job and for an overseas remote role, when a test task is a fair sample and when it is free work, and how to follow up without pestering. Philippine context throughout, including what changes when the employer is not in the country. No invented statistics about recruiters, no promises about callbacks, and nothing you cannot check for yourself.
outcomes: Turn duties you performed into evidence a stranger can check
Write a one page resume ordered for somebody reading fast
Assemble a portfolio that shows finished work, including when the work is confidential
Send an application that could only have been written for that role, and explain a gap or a credential in one honest line
Handle the expected pay question, an unpaid test task and the follow up without underselling or overpromising

modules.description: Before you write a word: how an application gets filtered, what counts as evidence rather than assertion, and which role you are actually aiming at. Every later decision comes from this chapter.

lessons.title: How your application gets filtered
lessons.content_mdx:
# How your application gets filtered

Riza screens hiring for a logistics company in Mandaue. One opening for an admin assistant, one folder of applications, and an hour before her next meeting. She is not going to read them. She is going to sort them.

Hold that distinction, because the rest of this course comes out of it. On a first pass nobody is deciding whether you are good. They are reducing a pile to something small enough to read properly, and the fastest way to reduce a pile is to look for a reason to set an application aside.

## Sorting is not evaluating

A sorting pass has a rough shape. A look at the top of the document, where your name and what you do should be. A quick check that you are plausibly for this role and not for some other one. Then a hunt for anything specific enough that it is still in her head when she reaches the bottom of the folder.

If nothing in your application survives that third step, you were not rejected. You were just not retained. Nobody made a judgement about you. There was nothing to hold onto.

Skill is not what the first pass is looking at, because Riza cannot see your skill. She can only see what you wrote down, and what you wrote down was "hardworking, fast learner, willing to be trained", which is also what the applications underneath yours say.

## Two different rooms

**A Philippine employer, reached through a job site or by email.** Assume the person opening your file is an HR generalist screening against a posting somebody else handed them. They are checking fit against that posting. Your job is to make the fit obvious rather than leaving them to construct it.

**An overseas remote posting.** Assume the reader is the person who would manage you, doing this between their own deliverables, working through replies that look near identical because they were written from the same template by people who never opened the posting. Nothing about you can be assumed. Not your school, not the company on your last line, not the fact that a certain firm in Ortigas is a serious place to have worked. Everything has to be legible on its own.

The documents you build for these two rooms are mostly the same. What changes is how much you have to spell out.

## The software in front of some employers

Some employers use software that receives, stores, sorts and searches applications. That much is true and worth knowing.

Here is what this course will not tell you, because nobody writing a lesson can know it: which product a given employer uses, whether it scores you, whether it rejects a file type, what a recruiter typed into its search box, or which layout survives a machine. Anybody selling you a guarantee about that is selling you a guess with a price on it.

What does survive being challenged is cheap, and none of it costs you anything:

- Plain structure. Ordinary headings, one readable column, no maze.
- The employer's own words for work you have genuinely done. If the ad says billing reconciliation and you did billing reconciliation, write billing reconciliation instead of the synonym you prefer. This is not keyword stuffing. Stuffing in terms you cannot back is the version that fails, and it fails in the interview, in front of somebody who asks.
- A file that opens on a stranger's machine, named with your name and the role.
- A link that opens without a request for access.

## The working rule

Your job on the first pass is not to be impressive. It is to be legible and specific, fast.

Legible means the reader can tell from the top few lines who you are and what you are for. Specific means there is at least one thing in there that could not have been written by anybody else applying to that job.

Test your own. Cover your name and read the top few lines of the resume you have now. If they would sit just as comfortably on the resume of the person at the next desk, they are doing nothing for you. Not because they are false. Because they do not distinguish.

Everything in the next two lessons exists to give you something true and specific to put up there. Lesson two is where you go and find it.

lessons.title: The evidence inventory
lessons.content_mdx:
# The evidence inventory

Before the resume, before the portfolio, before you answer a single posting, you open a blank file and spend an evening on this. Both documents are edits of it. Skip it and you will spend the next month rewriting adjectives and wondering why nothing lands.

## Everything you have finished

List it all, paid and unpaid. Jobs. Freelance gigs. School projects. Org work. The sari-sari store whose notebook you kept for your aunt. The parish page you ran for two years. The thesis whose data you cleaned. The despedida you coordinated because nobody else would.

Do not filter yet. Filtering is a later pass, and doing it now costs you the entries you have already talked yourself out of.

## Four columns

For every entry, fill in:

1. **What the task was.** The situation, in one line.
2. **What you personally did.** Not the team. You.
3. **What changed because of it.** What was different afterwards.
4. **What survives.** Something a stranger could actually look at.

Column four is what turns a list of memories into evidence, and it is the column everybody leaves blank.

## Duty against delivery

A duty is what the job description said. A delivery is what you produced.

"Handled customer inquiries" is a duty. Every support agent in the country can write it, so it tells a reader nothing about you.

Here is Kaye's delivery from the same job. She answered the shop's messages every morning so nothing sat overnight, and she wrote the standard replies for the questions that kept coming back, which the assistant who replaced her is still using. Column four: that reply file, and the message thread where the owner said the overnight backlog had stopped.

Same job, same year, same person. One version is furniture. The other is something Riza from lesson one can hold onto.

Run it on your own entries. Say what you did, then say what existed afterwards that did not exist before.

## Numbers only when they are yours

Put a number in only when you measured it yourself and could say where it came from if somebody asked. Kaye can say she cut the pending messages from around sixty a week to under ten, because she counted them every Friday. That is evidence. A figure you reverse-engineered so that it would sound bigger is a trap you set for yourself.

An inflated number is the one thing in your whole application that an interviewer can catch you on, and when it collapses it takes everything true in the same document down with it. That is a terrible trade for a figure that impressed nobody in the first place.

If you do not have the number, describe the change instead. "Nothing was left unanswered overnight" needs no arithmetic, and the owner who was there can confirm it.

## Save it now, into one folder

Access disappears. Company email closes on your last day. Group chats get archived. The client redesigns the site. The page you managed gets handed to somebody who clears it out.

Make one folder today and put in it: files you made and are allowed to keep, screenshots, links, the schedule you built, the report you wrote, the message where somebody said the work was good. Write the date and what each thing was for, because in eight months you will not remember.

Two rules while you do it. Take only what you are entitled to take, which is your own work and anything already public. Client lists, customer records and anything marked confidential stay where they are. Chapter two deals with how to show work you are not allowed to show, and taking it is not the answer.

If you are still in the job, ask now, while asking is easy. "I would like to keep a copy of the tracker I built, for my own portfolio. Is that alright?" That question is ordinary on the way out and awkward six months later.

## The empty rows

When you finish, some rows will be blank. A column four with nothing under it. A whole category with no entry at all.

That is not a verdict on you. It is a work list. If you want support roles and nothing survives that shows how you write to a customer, write one set of replies. If you want bookkeeping work and have nothing to show, offer to sort out one small set of books for someone you know, and keep the before and the after.

The inventory tells you what to go and make. Chapter two turns what is already in it into two documents.

lessons.title: The role you are aiming at
lessons.content_mdx:
# The role you are aiming at

Applying to everything is how you end up writing to nobody. The one-size application is not a shortcut. It is the thing that guarantees the reader finds nothing to hold onto, which is exactly the failure lesson one described.

So you pick first. Picking well takes one careful read of a real posting.

## Take one posting apart

Open an ad you would genuinely apply to, and answer four questions in your notes.

**What is the job, once the boilerplate is gone?** Skip the mission statement and the dynamic team. Read the duties. A posting titled Social Media Manager whose duties are answering customer messages, scheduling posts the marketing lead writes, and sending a weekly numbers report is a support and coordination job wearing a marketing title. Knowing that changes how you would answer it.

**Which requirements are the job, and which are the wishlist?** The ones repeated in the duties and echoed in the title are the job. The long list at the bottom is where wishes accumulate. Missing an item from that list is not a wall. Missing the thing the job actually is, is.

**What is the employer anxious about?** Somebody wrote that ad because they have a problem. Read the requirement lines as worries rather than rules. "Must work with minimal supervision" tells you that chasing people is on their mind. "Attention to detail is a must" tells you something went out wrong. Answer the worry and you are already ahead of the template replies.

**Which inventory entry answers it?** Go back to your file from lesson two and find the entry that speaks to that worry. If nothing in there does, this may not be your posting today.

## Two arrangements, not two versions of one

A job with a Philippine employer and an overseas remote engagement are different arrangements. Be exact about this, because people compare them as though they were the same thing with different numbers on it.

An employee of a Philippine company sits inside an employment arrangement. The employer runs payroll, handles the government contributions and the withholding, and there is a set of statutory benefits attached to that status, thirteenth month pay among them, that a contract rate does not come with. What each of those currently amounts to is for DOLE and the agencies to say rather than a course, and somebody else is administering them for you.

An overseas remote engagement is usually a contract, and inside a contract you are on your own. The rate is the whole of the compensation. Your equipment, your electricity, your connection, the days you cannot work, your own registrations and tax obligations, all of it sits behind that one figure. Nobody is deducting anything on your behalf and nobody is filing anything for you.

What each arrangement requires in law is not something to take from a course. Employment rules, contributions and tax obligations change, and each has an official source. DOLE, SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG and BIR publish what currently applies, and the contract itself is where you read what a client is offering. What you need from this lesson is the shape: a salaried offer and a contract rate are not the same kind of thing, and reading a contract as though it were an offer of employment is how people get surprised months later.

## Where you actually stand

Be honest about your position, because it decides where your hours go.

**Entry.** No paid experience in this line yet. Your leverage is the finished work in your inventory and how plainly you answer the posting.

**Already doing this.** You have delivered this exact work. Lead with it, name it in their words, and aim higher than you have been aiming.

**Shifting in.** You have real experience in something adjacent. Your task is to carry the delivery across, not to explain why you left. Chapter two has the language for that.

A stretch posting earns an application when you can answer the core of the job with evidence. It does not when all you can send is a plea. Twenty pleas take more of your week than four real applications and leave you with nothing at the end of it.

## The pay question starts here

Nobody has asked you yet. But the moment you decide to apply, you have already accepted whatever that role pays, and the arrangement it sits inside decides what the number has to cover.

So note it now. For each posting you keep, write down whether it is employment or a contract, and whatever the ad says about pay. Chapter three is where you answer the question once it is asked, with a range and a basis. Building the number itself, upward from what your own work costs you to do, belongs to Freelancing Fundamentals rather than to this course, and it is a different exercise from answering an interviewer.

quiz.prompt: Dennis has one resume he is proud of, and he has sent it unchanged to postings for admin assistant, HR assistant, virtual assistant and customer support. Three weeks in, nothing has come back. He asks a friend whether his resume is bad. What is the more useful diagnosis?

options.text: As a document it is probably fine. Nothing in it was written for any one of those postings, so no reader found anything to hold onto.
It is too thin for those roles, so he should add every job he has ever held and a longer summary until the page is properly filled.
Three weeks is too early to read anything into silence, so the sensible move is to keep sending the same file out and wait for replies.
The four roles are too different from one another, so he should choose one of them and send that same resume only to postings for it.

quiz.explanation: Riza is sorting, not evaluating. A document written for nobody in particular gives a sorting pass nothing specific to retain, which is why silence follows. Option d is tempting because narrowing is genuinely part of the answer, but narrowing while sending the same unchanged file changes nothing about what the reader sees. Option b makes it worse, since more general material is only more to skim past. Option c is comfortable because waiting requires no work, and it costs Dennis another three weeks of the same result.

quiz.prompt: A posting for a bookkeeping assistant in Iloilo lists five duties Charmaine has done for two years. A requirements list at the bottom names an accounting system she has never opened. She decides not to apply at all. What is she getting wrong?

options.text: Nothing. Applying without every listed requirement wastes the employer's time and her own on a role she was never going to be given.
The requirements list is decoration, so she can put the system on her resume and teach herself enough about it before anybody asks.
The system sits on a wishlist under duties she has actually performed, so the core of the job is answered and the application is worth sending.
She should apply only after teaching herself that system first, since the requirements list is where the employer says what it will test her on.

quiz.explanation: The requirements repeated in the duties are the job. A long list at the bottom is where wishes accumulate, and treating a wishlist item as a hard bar is how people rule themselves out of work they can do. Option a feels responsible and considerate, which is exactly what makes it dangerous. Option b takes the opposite wrong turn, and claiming a system you cannot use gets found out in the interview or in the first week, which puts every true line on the same resume in doubt. Option d is the patient version of the same error: an evening spent on a wishlist item is an evening not spent answering the duties she has already done, and the posting gets filled while she studies.

quiz.prompt: Nica ran the online orders for her cousin's milk tea shop for a year. She is choosing which inventory entry goes near the top of her resume for a customer support role. Which one belongs up there?

options.text: Managed all customer communications and daily operations for a growing food business, which covers the widest part of what she did.
Wrote the order and refund replies the shop still uses today, saved as a file of her own text that a stranger can open and read.
Trusted by the owner with complete responsibility for the shop's online presence, which shows how much she was relied on there.
Helped the business grow its online sales through a difficult year, which sets her contribution against the shop's overall result.

quiz.explanation: Column four of the inventory is the test: something survives that a stranger could look at. The reply file is checkable, is unmistakably hers, and is the exact work a support employer is hiring for. The other three are tempting because each one is true and each one sounds bigger. They are also unfalsifiable, so a reader has no way to weigh them and nothing to remember. Options a and c describe scope, while option d borrows credit from a result she cannot separate her own work from.

quiz.prompt: Arjun's tito tells him applications are thrown out by software unless the resume is ATS-optimised, and offers to sell him a template that is guaranteed to pass. Arjun's resume is a plain one-page document with clear headings. What should he do?

options.text: Buy the template, because a guarantee about software he cannot see the workings of is worth paying somebody who does see them.
Rebuild it as a two-column design with a graphic skills chart, so that a human reader is more likely to stop and look at it.
Rewrite every bullet in the ad's own phrasing, including three duties he has not performed, so the wording matches all the way down.
Keep the plain page, use the employer's own words for work he has really done, and check that the file opens on another machine.

quiz.explanation: Software does sit in front of some employers, and that is the honest end of what anybody can tell you. Which product, whether it scores, what a recruiter searched for and which layout survives are not knowable from outside, so a guarantee is a guess with a price on it. Option a is tempting because certainty is worth money when you feel blind. Option b is a real trade-off, though a heavy layout is harder to read either way. Option c is the one that sounds like the advice in this lesson and is not: their words go on work you have genuinely done, and three duties he has not performed are a claim somebody will ask him about.

quiz.prompt: Bianca is holding two things: an offer from a Manila company as a regular employee, and a posting from an overseas client for the same kind of work as an independent contractor at an hourly rate. She converts the hourly rate to a monthly figure, sees it is higher, and decides to take the contract. What is missing from her comparison?

options.text: Nothing is missing. Converting the hourly rate into a monthly figure puts the two on the same footing, and the higher figure wins.
A contract rate is the whole of her compensation and has to carry what an employer would otherwise administer, so the two do not compare.
Overseas contracts pay better than local employment as a rule, so the only thing left for her to check is whether the client pays on time.
Exchange rates move constantly, so she should hold off on the decision until the peso sits at a level that favours taking the contract.

quiz.explanation: An employment arrangement and a contract are different arrangements, not two versions of one. Inside employment, payroll, contributions and withholding are administered for her. Inside a contract the rate stands alone behind her equipment, her downtime and her own obligations, and what those obligations currently are is for BIR and the agencies to say rather than a course. Option a is the arithmetic everybody does, and it is arithmetic on two things that are not alike. Option c is a belief worth being suspicious of, and option d treats a real risk as the main question when the structure is the main question.

quiz.prompt: A posting is titled Social Media Manager. The duties under it are answering customer messages, scheduling posts the marketing lead writes, and sending a weekly numbers report. Rowena has done all three, in a support job. How should she read the posting?

options.text: The duties are the job and the title is packaging, so she applies against the duties using the support work that matches them.
The title is the job, so she should build the application around campaign strategy and planning to look like a manager.
The mismatch is a warning sign that the employer does not know what it wants, so the posting is better skipped for a clearer one.
She should apply and ask in the interview which of the two it really is, keeping the application general until she has an answer.

quiz.explanation: Strip the boilerplate and the duties tell you what the work is. Rowena has done that work, and answering the duties is what makes her application legible. Option b is the common mistake, because writing to the title means claiming a job she has not done while ignoring the one she has. Option c throws away a role she is well matched to over a title that cost the employer nothing to write. Option d keeps the application vague on purpose, which is the failure from lesson one, and the interview only happens if the application survives the sort.

quiz.prompt: Ella ran her college org's Facebook page. She wants to put grew engagement by 45 percent on her resume. She never tracked it, and the figure came from somebody's guess in the group chat. What should she write instead?

options.text: Keep the figure but soften it to grew engagement by roughly 45 percent, so it reads as an honest estimate rather than a measurement.
Drop the entry entirely, because unpaid college org work with no numbers behind it does not earn any space on a one-page resume.
Write significantly grew the page's engagement, which makes exactly the same point without committing her to a number she cannot prove.
Write what she did and what survives, which is the posting schedule she built and the three posts the page keeps pinned as examples.

quiz.explanation: An invented number is the one line an interviewer can catch you on, and when it falls it takes the true lines beside it down with it. Option a is tempting because rounding feels like honesty, but it is the same unsupported figure with a hedge in front of it. Option c is the phrase people reach for, and it trades a checkable claim for an adjective that a sorting reader skips. Option b throws away real evidence, since unpaid work counts and a schedule and a pinned post are things a stranger can open.

quiz.prompt: Beth has resigned and finishes in two weeks. The trackers, reports and templates she built over two years sit in her work email and on the company drive. She plans to sort out her portfolio next month, once the job hunt actually starts. What should she do before her last day?

options.text: Wait until the job hunt actually starts, then email her old manager and ask whether they can send over the trackers and reports she built.
Ask her manager for a reference letter instead, which covers the same ground and raises no awkward question about company files at all.
Save her own work that she is allowed to keep, ask about anything unclear while asking is still normal, and note what each file was for.
Rely on describing the work from memory, since a resume carries the description anyway and none of this material was ever confidential.

quiz.explanation: Access ends on the last day, and asking afterwards is a favour rather than a routine question. The move is to save what is genuinely yours and to ask about the rest now, while asking reads as ordinary. Option a is the one people actually plan on, and it turns a routine question into a favour: her manager has a job of their own, no obligation, and no reason to spend an afternoon in a leaver's folders. Option b is worth doing as well, but a letter is somebody's opinion rather than the work itself. Option d assumes memory holds file names and details for eight months, and it does not.

lessons.title: A resume that survives a skim
lessons.content_mdx:
# A resume that survives a skim

Joan has four years of admin and purchasing work in Bacolod. Her resume opens with "Objective: To secure a challenging position in a reputable company where I can maximise my potential and contribute to organisational growth." The line under it is her high school. Her best piece of work, rebuilding a supplier list nobody had cleaned in three years, sits on page two inside a paragraph.

Nothing about Joan is unqualified. She has put the reason to keep her where a fast reader will never find it.

Your resume has one job: give somebody moving quickly something specific in the first few lines. What follows is how to arrange the inventory you built in chapter one so that happens.

## The top of the page

Four things, in this order.

Your name. The role you are applying for, in the employer's own words: "Accounts Assistant" if that is what the ad says, not "Aspiring Finance Professional". A contact line that works, meaning a number you answer and an email address you would be happy to read aloud in an interview. Then two or three lines saying what you do and what you have done, written for this posting and rewritten for the next one.

Joan's version: "Admin and purchasing support, four years, hardware retail. Rebuilt the supplier list, ran the weekly reorder, closed the month with the bookkeeper." Not one adjective in it.

Cut the objective. It describes what you want. The reader is looking for what you have finished.

## Bullets built the same way every time

What you did, how, and what changed. Chapter one called that a delivery, and a resume bullet is a delivery cut down to one line.

Joan's worst bullet: "Responsible for supplier coordination." Her best: "Rebuilt the supplier list, matching every item to a current price and a lead time, so the reorder stopped going out against prices from three years ago." Same job, same year. Only the second one is hers.

Experience goes in reverse order, most recent first. Inside each job, relevance beats chronology: the bullet that answers this posting goes at the top of that job's list, not the one that happened most recently.

Numbers follow the rule the inventory set. Only what you measured yourself, and only where you could say out loud where the figure came from.

## The one page discipline

One page is not a rule handed down from anywhere. It is a constraint, and the reason to accept it is that it forces you to choose. The thing you want read first cannot be on the second page, because you do not control whether the second page is in front of the reader at all.

Cut in this order: the objective, adjectives with no evidence under them, tools you cannot open, seminars that changed nothing about what you can do, and duties that every other person with that job title also performed.

## Use their words, honestly

If the ad says "reconciliation" and you called it checking the bank against the book, write reconciliation. That is translating, and it costs you nothing.

If the ad names a tool you have never opened, leave it out. That is not translating, that is a claim, and the claim gets tested in week one.

## Photo, address, birthday

Read the form in front of you rather than a rule somebody posted in a forum. Where a Philippine employer's ad or application form asks for a photo, a birthdate or a full home address, those fields are ordinary here and you fill them in. An overseas application may ask for none of them, and some employers strip personal details out of a file before a human reads it. No single rule carries between the two rooms, so do two things instead.

Give exactly what the form in front of you asks for, and nothing beyond it. If a field is not there and the ad does not mention it, leaving it off costs you nothing at all.

And keep the two documents apart. A full home address, a birthdate and a photo sitting on a file you are emailing to strangers is personal information travelling further than it needs to. City and province tell a local reader what they need about whether you can get to the office.

## File hygiene, and what it is not

Chapter one said software sits in front of some employers, and that we are not going to tell you how it scores, because we do not know. So none of this is a promise. It is cheap insurance.

Name the file with your name and the role, so it survives being saved into a folder with forty others. Send something that opens on somebody else's machine. Keep it one column of readable text, because a two column layout with text boxes is a gamble you gain nothing from taking. Click every link in it yourself, from a browser you are not signed into.

## The last pass

Read your own resume as the person in chapter one: moving fast, sorting, looking for a reason to keep you.

Delete every line that could have appeared on anybody else's resume for the same job. If deleting a line costs you nothing, that line was costing you attention.

What survives is short, specific and yours. That is the document. Now do it again tomorrow for the next posting, because the top three lines change every time and the rest mostly does not.

lessons.title: A portfolio that shows work
lessons.content_mdx:
# A portfolio that shows work

Kim keeps the books for three small businesses in Davao. Asked for a portfolio, she sent a folder link. The hiring manager clicked it and got a screen asking her to request access. Kim saw the request two days later, approved it, and never heard back.

That is a portfolio failing before anybody looked at the work, and none of it was about the work.

The other one is a folder of screenshots with no explanation, which tells a stranger that something happened but not what you did.

## An exhibit is a piece plus a note

A portfolio is not a gallery. It is a small set of exhibits, and under each one sits a short note:

- What the situation was.
- What you were asked for.
- What you did.
- What happened after.
- Which part was yours, if the work was shared.

That last line matters more than people expect. Looking at good shared work, a stranger cannot tell whether you led it or carried the folders. Saying so unprompted reads as confidence, not modesty.

Three or four pieces with notes beat twenty without. The note is the part everybody skips, and it is the part that turns a screenshot into evidence.

## When the work is not yours to show

Work you did for an employer or a client is not automatically yours to publish. Four situations, one ladder.

**Ask.** Message the client: "I would like to show the reconciliation process I built for you in my portfolio, with your name and all figures removed. Is that all right?" It costs you one message, and it is the only fully clean option there is.

**Redact.** If they agree with conditions, or the work is yours but the details are not shareable, strip it. The client becomes "a logistics company in Paranaque". Real names come out. Order numbers and amounts are replaced with substitutes, and you say on the piece that they were substituted. Then flatten what you send to an image, or rebuild the sample fresh, so the thing you covered is not still sitting inside the file you handed over.

**Show the method, not the material.** For confidential work, exhibit the process: the checklist you follow, the folder structure, the steps in your monthly close. A process document gives away nothing about the client and demonstrates more than a screenshot does.

**Build a labelled sample.** No paid work yet, or nothing you can touch? Make something real for a business that exists, and label it a sample on the piece itself. A sample you announce is evidence. A sample you let somebody assume was paid work is a lie with a delay on it.

Two hard lines. Never show a client's confidential material to win a job, because the person you are showing it to is watching what you would do with theirs. And never present somebody else's work as yours. Whoever catches that will not tell you they caught it. You will simply not hear back, and you will think it was the market.

## Portfolios for jobs nobody calls portfolio jobs

- A bookkeeper shows a cleaned ledger with substituted figures and the reconciliation checklist beside it.
- A support agent shows three written replies: a refund refusal, an apology, and a first response to somebody furious.
- A virtual assistant shows a calendar system and a one page process document for the thing the client used to explain every week.
- A writer shows the brief next to the finished piece, so the reader can see what was asked for.

If you did the work, an artefact exists. It is usually a document, and you probably deleted the last one. Start keeping them in one folder from today.

## Where it lives

Anywhere it opens.

The test is not which platform you chose. It is this: a stranger with no account, on a phone, taps your link and sees the work. No sign in, no request for access, no notification sent to you. Send the link to a friend and watch them open it while signed out of everything.

One more thing. Once that link is on a resume, it is permanent. Resumes get forwarded months later by people you never met. Do not reorganise your folders and break the only address a hiring manager has for your work.

lessons.title: Gaps, credentials and honest framing
lessons.content_mdx:
# Gaps, credentials and honest framing

Marlon worked three years on a support account in Cubao, then left to care for his mother, who was ill for most of the following two years. He is applying again. Every draft of his application either invents a freelance business he never ran, or spends a full paragraph apologising.

Both are the same mistake. A gap is a fact, and facts get one line.

## The gap line

What the period was. What you did in it. Stop.

"From 2023 to 2025 I was my mother's full time carer. I took a bookkeeping course in the last six months of that and I am back working now."

No drama, no lesson about what the experience taught him, and no story that collapses the moment somebody asks one follow up question. Treat the gap question as a question mark to be closed rather than a trap to be survived. An unexplained two years is a question mark, and a question mark on a fast pass is a reason to move on.

Where it goes: the dates on your resume are honest, so they already show the gap. The one line belongs in the application message, or is said out loud in the conversation. It does not become a paragraph inside the resume, because that spends your best space explaining what you did not do.

## Changing direction

Shifting from one kind of work to another, lead with the delivery that transfers, not with why you left.

Nobody hiring is interested in the manager you could not work with. They want to know whether the thing you are good at survives the move. "Four years handling irate customers on a US account, now applying that to client onboarding" is a sentence about them. "I was burnt out and wanted a change" is a sentence about you, and it opens a conversation you cannot win.

No paid experience yet? Say what you have built and finished, and let the portfolio carry the rest. Do not label yourself entry level in your first line and ask the reader to lower their expectations before they have read anything.

## Stating a credential so it can be checked

A certificate is worth exactly what the reader can check. State four things: what it is, who issued it, what it required, and how to verify it.

A GN Academy credential is built for that. Each one carries a code, and the code resolves to a public page under `/verify` that anyone can open with no account. That page shows the holder's name, the certification, the date it was issued, whether it is active or revoked, and the competency scores from the assessment behind it. If you switch your public profile on, your page under `/talent` lists your credentials, each linking to its own verification page, alongside your headline, skills and portfolio pieces.

So write the line as: "Resume, Portfolio and Job Hunting, GN Academy, code RPJ-2026-000123", with the verification link printed on the certificate itself. A reader can check it without having to ask you for anything, which is the whole point.

Now the part nobody enjoys. A credential is evidence that you were assessed. It is not evidence that you have done the work, and it does not entitle you to a rate. It sits beside the portfolio. It does not replace it. Put two applicants side by side holding the same credential, and the one with a finished piece of work attached has something the other does not.

For describing AI skills in particular, AI Essentials for Work has a lesson called Talking about your AI skills honestly. This one does not repeat it.

## The five small lies

Each of these is easy, common, and detonates exactly when the job becomes real.

- **An inflated job title.** You were an admin assistant, not an operations manager. Reference checks are boring and specific.
- **A tool you cannot use.** It gets tested in week one, in front of people.
- **A stretched date.** You cover four blank months by extending a job. Now a payroll record disagrees with you.
- **A number you cannot support.** "Increased sales by 40 percent." How do you know that? Whose figure is it?
- **A borrowed portfolio piece.** The one thing you can be asked to walk through, line by line, on a call.

None of these get caught dramatically. They get caught quietly, and the real cost is not the job you lose. It is that you never learn which of your applications died of it.

## The tone for all of it

State the fact. Offer the evidence. Do not apologise, and do not oversell.

Marlon's line is not clever. It is true, delivered without flinching, and it takes one breath. That is what you are aiming for on every hard question in this process.

quiz.prompt: Cheska is applying for an inventory clerk role at a warehouse in Cabuyao. Her proudest achievement is a fundraising drive she led for her college org that filled a gym. Her most relevant is six months covering stock counts at a hardware store, which she found dull. What belongs at the top of her resume?

options.text: The fundraising drive, because it is the strongest single result she has and it shows the initiative any employer wants.
The stock counts, written as what she did and what changed, with the fundraising drive kept further down the page.
Both of them, under a summary line presenting her as a versatile candidate who would suit a wide range of roles.
The fundraising drive first, then the stock counts, so the reader meets the impressive item before the routine one.

quiz.explanation: The reader is sorting for fit, not ranking achievements. Six months of stock counts is the thing that answers this posting, so it goes where a fast pass will hit it. The fundraising drive is genuinely her best work, which is exactly why it is tempting, and it still belongs lower down where it adds colour rather than confusion. The versatile summary is the write-to-nobody failure from chapter one. Leading with the impressive item treats the reader as an audience to win over, when they are a person deciding quickly whether she is plausibly for this job.

quiz.prompt: Ernesto has fifteen years behind him and a resume running to two and a half pages. He says he has already cut everything he can. What is left includes an objective paragraph, a list of eleven seminars he attended, and bullets such as 'Responsible for daily operations'. What is the honest next cut?

options.text: Shrink the font and the margins so that exactly the same content fits into two pages instead of two and a half.
Accept the length, because fifteen real years will not fit on one page and cutting real experience is dishonest.
Move the older roles into a second document he can send on request, leaving the last five years in the resume.
Delete the objective, the seminar list, and every bullet that any other person with that job title could also write.

quiz.explanation: A duty bullet is a job title restated, so deleting it removes no information. The seminars and the objective describe attendance and intention rather than delivery. Shrinking the type is the most tempting option because nothing appears to be lost, but it cuts nothing and makes the page harder to skim. Accepting the length protects material that is not carrying any weight. Splitting into two documents makes the reader ask for the rest, which is a request a reader moving fast has no reason to send, so compress the older roles into one line instead.

quiz.prompt: A virtual assistant posting names a task management tool Hazel has opened exactly once, in a two hour trial. Everything else in the ad matches what she does daily. What goes in her skills section?

options.text: Leave that tool out, and name the tools she does run plus what she uses each one for, using the ad's own vocabulary.
List the tool, since she has technically used it once and can work through tutorials before an interview comes up.
List the tool with 'basic' written beside it, which is honest enough and keeps her from being filtered out too early on.
Leave the skills section off entirely, since a list of tools proves nothing and her experience section carries her.

quiz.explanation: A tool on your resume is a promise about week one, and week one happens in front of people. The two hour trial is tempting because it is technically true, and technically true is what every caught claim was. Writing 'basic' feels like a hedge, but the reader takes it as can use it, and Hazel still cannot. Dropping the whole section over-corrects: the skills line is where the employer's own words legitimately belong, and losing it costs her the honest matches she does have.

quiz.prompt: Kim pastes a folder link into her resume and sends it to eleven employers over two weeks. She then opens the link in a signed out browser and gets a screen asking the viewer to request access. What should she do?

options.text: Wait for the access requests and approve each one fast, which also shows her which of the eleven actually looked.
Leave it alone, because an employer who is genuinely interested will send a request and the request itself is a signal.
Open the sharing on that same link so it stops asking for access, check it signed out, and keep the address she sent.
Move the work to a new public link, then email all eleven employers a correction with the working address in it.

quiz.explanation: Fixing the permission at the same address repairs eleven resumes that are already out of her hands, which is why the signed out check matters more than the choice of platform. Waiting for requests looks like free information, but each one is a delay sitting in somebody else's inbox and a reader moving fast will not send one. Treating the obstacle as a filter for genuine interest is comforting and wrong. Moving to a new link is the right instinct with the wrong mechanism: it orphans every copy already sent, and the correction email arrives as an apology.

quiz.prompt: Arnel built a payroll tracker for a client in Iloilo. It is the best thing he has made. It holds real employee names and salaries, and his contract says the client's data is confidential. He wants it in his portfolio. What is the right move?

options.text: Send it only when an employer asks for a sample, since a private message to one person is not the same as publishing.
Ask the client for permission to show it with names and figures replaced, and exhibit the method instead if they refuse.
Blur the names and the salary column in a screenshot, which hides the confidential part and leaves the real work visible.
Describe it in a resume bullet and keep it out of the portfolio, since confidential work simply cannot be shown at all.

quiz.explanation: Asking costs one message and is the only fully clean route, and the fallback of showing his method gives away nothing. Sending it privately feels safer and is the usual version of this mistake: the contract does not care how many people saw it, and the employer is reading how he treats a client's data. Blurring is nearly right, but he still has not asked, and a blur laid over a live file can travel with the data underneath it. Refusing outright throws away two options he had.

quiz.prompt: Mikaela's portfolio is nineteen screenshots of social media graphics from her last job, posted as a grid with no text anywhere on the page. She is getting no replies to her applications. Which change is most likely to help?

options.text: Add more pieces to the grid, since nineteen is a thin body of work and a fuller page looks more like a professional's.
Post the same grid on a second platform as well, so that more of the people reading her applications come across it.
Replace the grid with a written list of every brand and campaign she worked on, which is much faster for a reader to scan.
Cut it to four pieces and put a short note under each: the brief, what she did, and what happened after it went out.

quiz.explanation: Nineteen screenshots prove that something happened and say nothing about what Mikaela did, so the note is the whole fix. Adding more is tempting because volume feels like proof, but more of the same carries no new information. A second platform spreads a piece that still says nothing. The written list is the trap worth naming: brand names read as impressive and are pure claim, since nobody can tell from a list which part of the work was hers.

quiz.prompt: Elaine was a teacher, then spent two years out of work during a family illness, and is now applying for a scheduling role. Her draft resume opens with a paragraph explaining the gap and why she left teaching. What should she do with that paragraph?

options.text: Cut it, open with what transfers from teaching, and keep one plain line about the gap for the message or the call.
Keep it in the resume but move it to the bottom, so the reader meets her experience first and the explanation after.
Cut it and let the dates speak for themselves, answering the gap question only if an interviewer raises it directly.
Keep it but cut it to two sentences, since a gap left unexplained reads like something she is trying to hide.

quiz.explanation: The resume's space is for delivery, and the gap needs one line somewhere a person is actually reading sentences. Moving the paragraph to the bottom keeps the resume doing a job it should not be doing. Letting the dates speak is half right and the most defensible wrong answer: the dates are honest, but an unexplained two years is a question mark on a fast pass, and one line removes it cheaply. Two sentences still aim the reader's attention at the two years instead of at what Elaine can do.

quiz.prompt: Bernard was an admin assistant for two years, and in that job he also arranged deliveries and built the staff schedule. A friend tells him to write Operations Manager on his resume, because it describes the work better and admin assistant undersells him. What should Bernard do?

options.text: Write Operations Manager, since job titles vary between companies anyway and his bullets underneath describe what he did.
Write Admin Assistant moving into operations, which reflects the direction the role was going without misstating it.
Keep Admin Assistant as the title and use the bullets to show the deliveries and the schedule he ran inside that job.
Ask his old employer whether they would describe him as operations, and use whichever title they say they would give.

quiz.explanation: The title is the one line on a resume that an employment record or a reference call can flatly contradict, and the work he actually did is safe in the bullets where it is checkable. Rewriting the title is tempting precisely because titles really are inconsistent between companies, which makes it feel like a translation rather than a claim. The hybrid smuggles in a promotion that did not happen. Asking the old employer is a good instinct badly aimed: an informal description does not change the record, and it puts them in an awkward position.
