lessons.title: The application nobody else sent
lessons.content_mdx:
# The application nobody else sent

Marilou is applying for an admin assistant post at a dental clinic in Marikina. The ad says the clinic is moving its appointment book from paper to an online calendar, and whoever is hired will run it. Marilou set up and ran the shared calendar at her barangay health center for two years.

She sends the letter she sends everywhere. It opens with "Dear Sir/Madam, I am writing to express my keen interest in the position advertised," and it never mentions a calendar.

She was the right person. Nothing in her message said so.

## Three parts, and nothing else

**One: the role, and where you saw it.** One line. A clinic can be hiring for three things at once, and the reader should not have to work out which pile you belong in.

**Two: one thing from the posting, answered with one thing you have done.** Not your proudest achievement. The one that matches the thing they wrote the ad about. Then say where it can be seen.

**Three: what happens next.** Name what you attached, name the link, give a real availability for a call. Stop there.

Here is Marilou's middle paragraph, written twice.

Generic: "I am a hardworking and detail-oriented person with excellent organizational skills and a genuine passion for helping people."

Specific: "You mentioned moving the appointment book online. I set up and ran the shared calendar at our barangay health center for two years, including the double-booking rules and the reminder routine the midwives still use. There is a one-page write-up of how it works in the folder linked below."

Both are true about Marilou. Only one of them could have been written by her, about this job.

## What to cut

- The greeting to nobody. Use a name if the ad carries one, "Hiring team" if it does not.
- The paragraph about your passion. Nobody can check it, so it carries no information.
- The restatement of your resume. It is attached. They can read it.
- The closing that thanks them for their time and asks for nothing.

## The parts that get seen first

On email, the subject line and the opening line may be all that exists before anyone decides to open anything. Put the role and your name in the subject: "Application: Admin Assistant, Marilou Santos". Make the first line the role and the specific thing, not a greeting that spends the line saying hello.

Attach what they asked for, with your name and the role in the filename. Link the rest. Then open your own link in a browser where you are not signed in to anything. If it asks a stranger to request access, your application is finished, and nobody will write to tell you.

## When the application is a box

Some employers never receive an email from you at all. The application is a form on a job site, the letter is a field with a limit, and there is nowhere to attach anything.

Write the same three parts, shorter. Put the link in as plain text so it survives a form that strips formatting. If the form asks a question, answer that question first, then use the rest of the box for the specific thing you did.

Proposals on freelance marketplaces and cold outreach to businesses work differently and belong to Freelancing Fundamentals. Platform mechanics such as fees, credits, ranking and badges change often enough that printing them here would only mislead you, so read the current help pages of whichever site you are on.

## When it is a chat, or a piece of paper

A Philippine employer may post the vacancy on their page and ask you to send your resume through Messenger, or ask you to bring a printed copy in. The three parts do not change. What changes is what you can attach and how long the reader stays.

In a chat there is no subject line, so the first line does both jobs: the role, and the one thing you have done about the thing they wrote the ad about. Send the file as a file rather than as pasted text, and put the link underneath as plain text, because a link that opens for somebody signed in to nothing is still your best evidence.

On paper, assume the copy leaves with them and you do not. Your name and the role sit at the top, your contact line sits where a thumb finds it, and anything that does not fit belongs behind a link short enough to be typed by hand.

## Drafting with AI

Fine as a drafting engine. Fatal as an author.

A model can tighten your sentences, cut your length, and tell you which paragraph says nothing. It cannot supply the calendar at the barangay health center. A message assembled entirely from a model's idea of an application letter is, by construction, the message everyone else sent, which is the exact failure this lesson exists to prevent.

The rule: every concrete fact in the message comes from you. Basic AI and AI Essentials for Work cover the drafting craft itself.

## Try this

Open the last posting you saved and write the middle paragraph only. One sentence naming something from the ad. One naming what you have done about that thing. One naming where it can be seen. If you cannot write the second sentence, either you are applying to the wrong posting or you have work to go and finish first.

lessons.title: The money question and the test task
lessons.content_mdx:
# The money question and the test task

Two moments decide what the work will be worth, and both of them happen before anybody hires you.

Dianne is interviewing for a marketing assistant post at a company in Ortigas. Twenty minutes in: "What are your salary expectations?" Ken is on a call with a founder in Melbourne about a part-time remote operations role, and gets the same question. Same words, different arrangement. Answering them the same way is how one of the two ends up short.

## They are not the same question

Chapter one drew the line between the two arrangements. Here is what that line does to a number.

Inside employment, the figure you are discussing sits within everything the employer administers around it, and it is not the whole of what you get. Inside a contract there is nothing around the number. Your machine, your connection, the weeks with no work, and your own registrations and tax obligations all sit inside it. If you register as a freelancer here, filing on a schedule comes with the registration, and the current rules, rates and deadlines are published by the offices that run them. Look them up there, not in a group chat.

So the flat rule: never take a local salary, or a foreign figure converted at today's exchange rate, and quote it into the other arrangement as though the same things were covered.

## Answer with a range and a basis

Three answers are available to you, and only one of them works.

**A bare number**, named blind because refusing felt rude. You are now anchored to a figure you cannot explain, and if it is low you will be held to it for a year.

**No answer at all.** "I am flexible." "Whatever is standard." It sounds accommodating. It hands the decision to the person across from you and tells them nothing about how you think.

**A range, and one sentence of basis.** "For a full-time role at this scope I am looking at this much to this much a month. That comes from current postings for the same responsibilities in Metro Manila, and it assumes the schedule and the review period you described."

Building the number itself, from what your work costs you to produce and what it has to cover, is a longer job, and Freelancing Fundamentals teaches it. What this course asks is narrower: arrive with the range already worked out, be able to say where it came from in one sentence, and know what the arrangement covers so you know what your number has to carry.

Two habits make that possible. Research current postings for the actual role in the actual market before the call, never during it. And write your floor down beforehand, the figure below which the answer is no, so you are not deciding that while trying to be liked.

## The test task

The freelance version of this, where a client asks for the live deliverable before anything is agreed and the counter is to offer a small paid first piece, is in Freelancing Fundamentals under Where the work actually comes from. What follows is the hiring-process version, where the counter is different because there is no contract to negotiate yet.

A fair sample is small, scoped, described before you start, and the same for every candidate. Two replies to a made-up complaint. Half a page in their template. A short call plan for a fictional client.

Free work looks different. It is a real deliverable, with a real deadline, often on a client's live material, and it ships whether or not you are hired. Twelve product descriptions for a store that goes live on Monday is not a sample of your work. It is Monday's work.

The reply that tells one from the other is not an accusation. Ask four things: what exactly is being asked for, what it is judged on, how long they expect it to take, and what happens after they read it.

An employer who has thought about the task answers that in a few lines. Somebody collecting free work goes vague or goes quiet. Either way you have learned something, and asking is itself a demonstration. Agreeing scope before starting is the job, and doing it politely at this stage is a sample of how you will behave in week three.

## The trap at the end

The trap is not the unfair test. It is agreeing to something you cannot deliver because saying so felt awkward.

Ken says yes to a two-day turnaround while a full week of other work is already sitting in front of him. He has just made his first promise to this employer, and it is one he is going to break. A hiring process where you overpromise once becomes a working relationship where you overpromise weekly.

## Once you have accepted a fair one

Work to the brief you were given, including the time in it. If the task says about forty five minutes, forty five minutes is what is being sampled, and an afternoon of polish answers a question nobody asked. It also promises a standard you cannot hold once real deadlines arrive, which is the overpromise above wearing better clothes.

If the brief is unclear, ask before you start rather than after. That is the same move as the four questions, and it is still free.

## Try this

Write two sentences now, before anybody asks you. One is your range and its basis for a local salaried role. One is your range for a contract where nothing is covered except the work. Keep them in the same file as your evidence inventory, and update them every time you finish a piece of work worth adding.

lessons.title: The conversation, and what happens after
lessons.content_mdx:
# The conversation, and what happens after

Joel gets the call back. Fifteen minutes in, the interviewer asks him to describe something he handled that went wrong. Joel says he is a fast learner who works well under pressure. The interviewer writes nothing down.

An interview is your evidence, spoken. Nothing new is needed. What is needed is being able to say three entries from your inventory out loud, in order, without wandering.

## Three stories, short arcs

Pick three before the call and match them to what the ad emphasised. For each one: what the situation was, what you did, what happened afterwards.

Say each one aloud once. If you cannot get to the end without backing up to explain something, the story needs cutting, not more detail. Do not memorise a script. A rehearsed speech sounds rehearsed, and it falls apart at the first follow-up question.

## When you do not know

Say so, then say what you would do about it. "I have not used that one. I used a different tool for the same job at the clinic, and I would spend the first day in their documentation and ask whoever set it up what the conventions are."

Bluffing does not get caught on the call. It gets caught in week two, by the person who hired you because of the bluff.

## The questions you ask

Your questions are read as closely as your answers, so ask the ones somebody planning to do the work would ask.

- What does the first month look like for whoever takes this?
- How is the work reviewed, and by whom?
- Who would I be reporting to day to day?
- What would good look like in this role by the end of the year?

## If the employer is not in the country

Four things need concrete answers rather than reassurance.

**Hours.** Name the overlap you can hold every single week, not the one you managed twice last month.

**Setup.** What machine you work on, and what connection you have at home.

**Backup.** This is the one people fumble, because they try to promise that nothing will ever go wrong. Nobody believes that, and the first brownout turns it into a lie. Say what you actually do instead: a phone with data on it, a coworking space or a relative's house nearby, and a message sent within a set time whenever something goes down.

**Days off.** Name the days you do not work, and let them tell you how that fits their week. Guessing at somebody else's calendar helps nobody.

## The follow-through is the sample

Everything you do between applying and being hired is a free preview of how you work.

- Reply within a reasonable time. If a proper answer needs a day, send a line saying so.
- Send what you said you would send, by when you said it. If it is going to slip, say so before the date, with a new date attached.
- Be on the call early, somewhere you can be heard.
- Follow up once, after the interval they named. If nobody named one, ask at the end of the call so that you have one.

When the answer is silence, one short message early the following week is the whole move. When the answer is no, two lines: thanks for letting me know, and you would be glad to hear from them if something that fits comes up later. It costs a minute, and the person turning you down today may be the same person hiring in six months.

## The tracker

A search runs for weeks and memory does not. One sheet, one row per application: where, what role, the date you sent it, what you sent, what they said, what is due next and when.

It stops you applying twice to the same place, it stops you forgetting the sample you promised on a call, and after a month it shows you which kinds of application actually get answered.

## The loop

Every application produces new evidence. A sample you built for a test task, a write-up you made for one clinic, a question that exposed a gap you can now go and fill. All of it goes back into the inventory from chapter one, which is a living file rather than an exercise you did once.

## Try this

Make the tracker today, with the last three things you applied for already in it, and one line under each saying what you owe that employer next and by when. If the answer is nothing, write nothing. That is a row you can stop thinking about.

quiz.prompt: Marilou has one cover letter she has polished over several evenings, and it reads well. Tonight she has an hour and four saved postings, one of them a dental clinic whose ad says it is moving its paper appointment book online. Marilou ran the shared calendar at her barangay health center for two years. What is the best use of the hour?

options.text: Send the polished letter to all four postings tonight, since one general letter reaching four employers beats one slower application.
Send the polished letter to the clinic first, then spend the rest of the hour finding more postings to send that same letter to.
Keep the polished letter for all four, but add one line about her passion for healthcare so that each of them feels personal.
Send the clinic one letter naming the calendar she ran and where it can be seen, then apply to the other three on another night.

quiz.explanation: The clinic wrote its ad around one worry, and Marilou has already done that exact thing. A paragraph naming the calendar, with somewhere it can be seen, is the only version of tonight that could not have been sent by anybody else. Option a is tempting because volume feels like effort, but a letter written for nobody arrives as a letter from nobody. Option b spends the saved time widening a message that was never specific. Option d adds a sentence nobody can check, which is not the same as adding evidence.

quiz.prompt: Dianne is interviewing for a marketing assistant role at a company in Ortigas. She has read current postings for the same responsibilities and has a range in mind, but when the interviewer asks about her salary expectations, naming a figure suddenly feels presumptuous. What should she say?

options.text: Say she is flexible and open to whatever the company's standard is for the role, so that the offer does not slip away.
Give the range, one sentence on where it came from, and what she has assumed about the scope and the review period.
Ask the interviewer to name the budget for the role first, and give no figure of her own until that has happened.
Name the very top of her range as a single flat figure, since a range only invites them to pick the bottom of it.

quiz.explanation: A range with a basis is an answer the other side can work with, and the basis is what stops it sounding like a wish. Option b feels gracious and is a common instinct, but it hands the decision away and says nothing about how she thinks. Option c is a fair thing to ask once, though refusing to answer until they go first turns a conversation into a standoff. Option d throws away the room a range gives her to explain what the number has to cover.

quiz.prompt: Ken is employed by a Philippine company and is talking to a founder overseas about a part-time remote contract. Asked for his rate, he plans to quote his current monthly salary, because he would be happy earning the same as he earns now. What is wrong with that plan, and what should he do?

options.text: His salary sits inside an arrangement the contract will not carry, so he should rebuild the figure and quote that range instead.
Nothing is wrong with the figure, so he should quote it and ask for a review after three months once he has proved himself.
He should convert that same salary into the founder's currency at today's rate, so that the number reads as normal in their market.
He should quote the same figure and then ask the founder to cover his internet and his equipment as a separate monthly allowance.

quiz.explanation: A salary is one part of an arrangement that also handles payroll, contributions and leave. A contract rate carries the work plus everything that arrangement used to absorb, including his equipment, his unpaid weeks, and his own registration and filing. Option a ports the number and postpones the problem to a review that may never come. Option b converts a figure whose meaning does not survive the conversion. Option c is closer, because it notices something is missing, but it patches two visible costs and leaves the invisible ones out.

quiz.prompt: Jomar applies for a virtual assistant role with a small online store. The reply asks him to write product descriptions for twelve items that go live on Monday, unpaid, so they can see how he works. He wants the job and does not want to look difficult. What should he do?

options.text: Write all twelve well and send them on time, since arguing at this stage costs him a job that he actually wants and needs.
Decline it, because any unpaid task is free work and a business that asks for one is not worth working for anyway.
Ask what exactly the task is judged on, how long they expect it to take, and what happens after they have read what he sends.
Write three of the twelve and say the rest can follow once there is a signed agreement and a start date in place.

quiz.explanation: Twelve items with a launch date behind them is Monday's work, not a sample, but the useful move is to clarify rather than to accuse. Those questions take a few lines to answer for anybody who has thought about the task, and the answer tells him which of the two this is. Option a hands over a deliverable and teaches them what he will accept. Option c refuses a fair sample along with an unfair one. Option d negotiates a smaller amount of free work without ever finding out what is being tested.

quiz.prompt: The overseas founder asks Ken whether he can be online from nine in the evening to five in the morning, Philippine time, every weekday. Ken could manage those hours some nights but not reliably every night, and he badly wants the role. What is the right answer to give?

options.text: Say yes, since he can hold it for the first few weeks and can raise the difficulty later once he has proved he is useful.
Say which hours he can hold every week without fail, then ask which parts of their day actually need him online and present.
Say yes but plan to be on his phone during the hours he cannot properly work, so that he is at least reachable throughout the night.
Say the schedule is impossible for him and ask whether the whole role could be done on his own hours with no overlap at all.

quiz.explanation: The commitment you can hold every week is worth more than the one you can hold until you are tired, and asking which hours matter often shrinks the requirement to something real. Option a buys the job with a promise that breaks in month two, when breaking it is expensive. Option c is the same promise with a worse version of the work behind it. Option d is honest, but it skips the question that would have found the overlap that actually works.

quiz.prompt: At the end of a good interview, Joel offered to send a one-page write-up of the handover process he built, and said it would arrive Tuesday. On Monday night an unrelated deadline lands and the write-up will not be ready before Thursday. What should he do?

options.text: Send whatever he has on Tuesday, because arriving on the promised day matters more to a new employer than the state of it.
Send it Thursday with an apology attached, since flagging a delay in advance only draws attention to the fact he is late.
Message them on Monday naming Thursday as the new date, then send it on Thursday exactly as he has just said he would.
Say nothing and drop it, since he offered it himself rather than being asked, and raising it now creates a problem.

quiz.explanation: Nothing he does here is really about a write-up. It is the employer's first sample of what he does when one of his own dates is in trouble, and the answer they want is early warning followed by a date that then holds. Option a trades the thing he is being judged on for punctuality. Option b is the common instinct and it is backwards, because a warning is a courtesy while a silent overrun is a surprise. Option c assumes they forgot, and anybody who did not forget now has a data point.

quiz.prompt: Marilou's interviewer said the clinic would decide by the end of the week. Friday passes with no word, and so does the weekend. She is anxious, the role suits her, and she has two other applications still open. What should she do on Monday?

options.text: Send one short message asking where the decision stands, then leave it there and keep working on her other applications.
Message every second day until somebody answers, since the applicant who stays visible is the one they end up remembering.
Treat the silence as a no, stop thinking about the clinic, and never contact them again about this or a later role.
Wait another full week before saying anything, since chasing a decision that is already late is what loses a candidate the offer.

quiz.explanation: One message after the interval they themselves named is a fair ask, and stopping after it is what keeps it fair. Option b is tempting because waiting feels passive, but repeated chasing is a preview of how she will handle a client who is slow to reply. Option c is the quiet version of the same anxiety, and it costs her a role that may still be open. Option d is the opposite instinct and costs her the same week: they named the interval themselves, it has passed, and one message inside it is the thing she is entitled to send.

quiz.prompt: After a second interview, Ken gets a two-line email saying the company went with somebody else. He is disappointed, he thought it went well, and it is a company he would still like to work for someday. What is the best reply?

options.text: Ask for detailed feedback on why he was not chosen and which part of the interview process he actually lost it on.
Reply setting out the two things he thinks he answered best in the second interview, in case the decision was closer than it looked.
Send nothing at all, since a reply to a rejection changes nothing and takes attention away from applications still open.
Reply in two lines, thanking them for the time and saying he would be glad to hear about anything that fits him later.

quiz.explanation: Two warm lines cost a minute and leave the door open with somebody who has already met him and may be hiring again. Option a is understandable and sometimes works as a light ask, but framed as a demand for detail it puts work on a person who owes him none. Option b reopens a decision that has already been made, politely and at length, and a reply that asks to be reconsidered is the one they remember him by. Option d is not rude, it is just the option that throws away the only thing left on the table.

final_exam.title: Resume, Portfolio and Job Hunting final exam

questions.prompt: Trina works for a firm in Ortigas that everybody in her industry here recognises, and she is applying to a remote posting with a company in another country. The top of her resume leads with the firm's name, her university, and the fact that she was promoted twice in three years. What is the risk in leading with those three?

options.text: Nothing much, since a known employer and a good university are the fastest signals of quality that a reader anywhere can pick up.
Two promotions in three years read as somebody expensive, so the money conversation starts before they have seen anything she did.
It reads as boasting to a foreign employer, and the tone of the opening lines is what decides whether the rest of the page gets read.
A reader abroad cannot decode any of them, so her best space goes on names that carry nothing there and no work she has finished.

questions.explanation: In the second room nothing about you can be assumed. The firm everybody here recognises is a name, the university is a name, and a promotion is a fact about an internal ladder whose rungs a stranger cannot see. Everything has to be legible on its own, so the top of the page carries what she did and what changed because of it, with the firm's name still sitting there and no longer being asked to do the work. Option b is what prestige is assumed to do for you, and it holds in one room and not in the other. Option c invents a motive for the reader that nothing in the posting supports. Option d treats the problem as tone, when the problem is that three lines have gone by carrying nothing a reader abroad can use.

questions.prompt: An ad for an accounts assistant in Valenzuela puts attention to detail in the title line, in three of the six duties, and again at the bottom. Reymar has two years of encoding delivery receipts and has never once described himself in those words. What should he take from the repetition?

options.text: That something went out wrong there before, so his opening should name the receipts he encoded and the errors he caught in them.
That the phrase is filler in almost every ad, so it carries nothing at all and he should write his application from the duties alone.
That they want somebody who describes themselves that way, so the phrase belongs in his opening line in their own words.
That the bar sits above what he can evidence, so the evening is better spent on a posting that does not lean on the phrase.

questions.explanation: Somebody wrote that ad because they have a problem, so a requirement repeated three times reads as a worry rather than a rule. Answering the worry is what makes his opening line his: the receipts he encoded and the errors he caught in them are the same claim with evidence under it. Option b is the near miss and stops one step short, because repeating their phrase back is an adjective anybody applying can also type. Option a throws away the clearest signal in the ad. Option d rules him out of a posting his two years already answer, which is the wishlist mistake in a different costume.

questions.prompt: An overseas remote posting for a customer support role has one required field: expected hourly rate. Grace has only ever been paid a Philippine salary and has no idea what to type. She is about to write the word negotiable so she does not price herself out of the shortlist. What belongs in that field?

options.text: Her current monthly salary converted at today's rate and divided by her working hours, which keeps her honestly at the level she is paid now.
The lowest figure she could live on, since being the cheapest candidate is the one clear advantage she has over people the client knows already.
The word negotiable, because naming any number before she knows what the client has budgeted can only cost her the interview she wants.
A range she can justify in one line, taken from what postings for this same remote role are currently offering, and priced as a contract.

questions.explanation: Two ideas have to meet here. A rate on a contract is the whole of your compensation: your own equipment, your own unpaid time between jobs, and your own registrations and obligations, whatever those currently are, all sit inside it, which a salary does not. And the way you answer is a range with its basis, not a bare number and not a refusal. Converting a salary feels honest and quietly imports an arrangement that does not apply. Naming the lowest number she could survive on sets the ceiling for the whole engagement and reads as somebody who has not priced the work. Negotiable is the answer that box collects all day, and it leaves the reader nothing to act on. Go and read current postings for the actual role in the actual market before filling it in.

questions.prompt: Two days after applying, Rosalie gets a reply asking two things: whether she could start by the fifteenth, and whether she has ever run a monthly stock count. She has run stock counts. She cannot answer the date honestly until she has checked her notice period with her current employer, which will take a day. What should she do?

options.text: Answer both within the hour with her best guess at the date, since she can go back and correct it later if her employer needs notice.
Wait until she has the real date and then send one complete reply, because an answer arriving in pieces reads as disorganised.
Reply the same day naming when she will have the date, answer the stock count question in that message, and come back on that day.
Answer the stock count question now and leave the date out, since raising a start date she is unsure of invites a harder one.

questions.explanation: Nobody has seen her work yet, so what she does with a small question is the sample they are actually reading. Reply inside a reasonable time, and where the real answer needs a day, say so and name the day, then keep it. Option b is the tempting one, because a complete answer feels more professional than a partial one, and what the employer has meanwhile is silence from somebody they have already written to. Option a buys a fast reply with a date she may have to take back, which makes her first promise to them one she breaks. Option c answers the half she finds easy and leaves them to chase the half they asked about first.

questions.prompt: Lorna keeps the books for two small clients. A posting asks applicants to attach samples of their work. Everything she has is a live client ledger carrying real names, amounts and account numbers, and neither client has been asked about any of it. What should she attach?

options.text: A short note on how she runs a monthly reconciliation, plus a small ledger she built herself with invented rows, labelled clearly as a sample.
One ledger rebuilt into a fresh file with the same structure and the real figures retyped, since what she sends is then not the client's own file.
One ledger with the client's name taken out of the header, since amounts and account numbers on their own do not identify anybody in practice.
Nothing, with a line saying bookkeeping is confidential work that produces no portfolio, and an offer to answer any questions they have.

questions.explanation: The order to work through is ask permission, redact, describe the method, or build a labelled sample. She has not asked, so what she can honestly send today is the method plus something she made herself and says she made. Retyping the real figures into a fresh file changes the container and not the contents: the amounts, the dates and the names are still the client's, she still has not asked, and the person who notices will not tell her they noticed. Removing the name from the header is worse than it looks: amounts, dates and account numbers together still identify, and a half redaction shows she does not know where the line sits. Sending nothing is honest and hands the reader nothing, and the premise is wrong anyway. A reconciliation process and a clean set of books are exactly the exhibit.

questions.prompt: An application form for a Philippine employer offers one box, headed why are you applying, with a short character limit. Ivan is about to paste the paragraph he uses everywhere, which opens by calling him a passionate and driven professional seeking growth. What should go in the box instead?

options.text: The role and where he saw it, one requirement from the posting, one finished thing of his that answers it, and what he is asking for next.
The strongest paragraph out of his resume summary, since it is already written and it is the best short description of him that exists.
A line saying his resume and portfolio are attached, so that the box does not repeat what the reader is about to open in a moment anyway.
A short account of why this industry has interested him since college, since an employer hiring for the long term is looking for real interest.

questions.explanation: The test for that box is whether the paragraph could have been sent to any other employer. If it could, it is doing nothing. Naming one requirement and answering it with one finished thing proves he read the posting, which is the cheapest way to be remembered. The resume summary is the most tempting option because it is polished and it is his, but the reader is about to read it anyway and a repeat wastes the one chance the box gives him. Pointing at the attachment gives the box away entirely and assumes the attachment gets opened. The passion paragraph is the default everybody sends, and interest in an industry is not evidence he can do the work. The finished thing is.

questions.prompt: A posting for a remote virtual assistant with an overseas agency states a monthly figure and describes the work as an independent contract. Ruth is salaried at a Philippine company now, likes the figure at first sight, and plans to sort the money out later if they make her an offer. What should she do tonight, before she writes anything?

options.text: Apply now and open the money question once they have decided they want her, since a candidate has no leverage before that point.
Work out whether that figure, standing alone as a contract rate, covers what she would be carrying herself, and note it down.
Apply now and ask in her first message whether the figure is negotiable, so she knows where it can move before she prepares more.
Skip it for postings that state no figure at all, since a printed rate is a ceiling and silence leaves the number open.

questions.explanation: The moment you decide to apply you have accepted whatever that role pays, so the arithmetic belongs before the application and not after the offer. A contract rate stands alone: her equipment, her connection, the weeks with no work, and her own registrations and obligations all sit inside that one figure, where a salary has an employer administering things around it. What those obligations currently amount to is for BIR and the agencies to say, and all this lesson asks is that she knows the figure has to carry them. Option b is the common plan, and it postpones a decision she has already made by applying. Option c is not a wasted question, it just asks about movement in a number she has not worked out yet. Option d treats a stated figure, which is information she can use tonight, as a reason to walk away.

questions.prompt: In a video interview for an admin role, the manager asks Cherry how she would set up an approval flow inside a system she has never opened. She understands approval flows and has built one by hand, but she does not know that product at all. What is the best answer?

options.text: A confident general answer about how approval flows work, since the concept transfers and naming the gap only plants a doubt about her.
That she has not used that product, then the approval flow she did build by hand, and what she would read or ask to get it working there.
The approval flow she built by hand, described in full, with no mention of the product at all, so she stays on ground she can defend.
A request to come back to it later in the call, so that she can quietly look the product up while the manager moves on to the next question.

questions.explanation: Saying what she does not know, and then saying what she would do about it, is the answer that survives the first week of the job. It also lets her spend the rest of the answer on evidence, which is the part she has. The confident general answer is tempting because it sounds capable and nobody can check it in the moment, but bluffing is the answer that gets checked later, in front of the person who then has to fix it. Describing the flow she built and never touching the gap is the near miss, and it is all true: it also leaves the question the manager actually asked, about a product she has not opened, sitting in the room for somebody else to raise. Stalling in order to look it up is the same bluff with extra steps, and a manager who has run interviews before watches it happen.

questions.prompt: An overseas employer asks Paolo in the interview about his internet, his power supply and which of their morning hours he can work. He is in Davao on a fibre line, in an area that has brownouts every few weeks. What should he say?

options.text: That his connection is solid and he has never had an outage, since raising brownouts now hands them an easy reason to choose somebody else.
The actual setup, what he does when the power or the signal drops, and the specific hours of their morning he can be online every day.
That he will make any hours work and be online whenever they need him, since flexibility is what gets a remote candidate picked over others.
That he will flag any outage the moment it happens, and let them tell him afterwards which of their morning hours they need him for.

questions.explanation: Remote employers are not looking for somebody with no problems. They are looking for somebody who has thought about theirs. A named backup and a specific overlap window is concrete enough to plan around, and it is the same habit the job will need every week. Promising perfect reliability is tempting and it lasts until the first brownout, at which point he has an outage and a broken claim. Promising any hours they need is how people agree to a schedule they cannot hold, and the first missed morning is then a broken promise rather than an inconvenience. Promising to flag an outage is a habit rather than a backup, and handing the hours question back to them leaves the two things they asked about, his plan and his overlap, for somebody else to work out.

questions.prompt: Analyn is filling in the fourth column of her evidence inventory for a year of doing the schedule at a family restaurant. Under what changed she has written that shifts stopped clashing. Under what survives she has written nothing, because the roster lived in a notebook that stayed with the restaurant. What should she do about that row?

options.text: Leave the row as it is, since what changed is the part an employer cares about and the notebook was never hers to take away.
Drop the row from the inventory, because an entry with nothing checkable under it is the unsupported claim this course warns about.
Ask the restaurant to photograph the notebook pages for her, and use those as the artefact even though the staff names are on them.
Rebuild one month of that roster in a fresh file, label it on the piece as work she is reconstructing, and put it in column four.

questions.explanation: Column four is what turns a memory into evidence, and an empty one is a work list rather than a verdict on the year. She cannot take the notebook, so she makes something a stranger can open: the same roster rebuilt, and said on the piece to be a rebuild. A sample you announce is evidence, and one you let a reader assume was the original is a lie with a delay on it. Option a leaves her with a change nobody can weigh, which is the row every inventory is full of already. Option b throws away a year of real work over an artefact she can still make this week. Option d carries other people's names out of a business that never offered them, and a reader looking at those names learns what she would do with theirs.

questions.prompt: A local agency sends every shortlisted applicant the same test: one product description, in your own words, and it should take about forty five minutes. Dexter wants the job badly and plans to spend a whole afternoon on it and send three different versions. What is wrong with that plan?

options.text: Only the three versions. More care on the sample can only make a better impression, so the fix is to send the strongest one he writes.
Unpaid work should always be held to the smallest possible amount, and forty five minutes is already more than an applicant should give.
The test asks what he can do in forty five minutes, so an afternoon answers a different question and hides how he works to a deadline.
The agency is timing him without saying so, and going over the stated time is the thing they are really screening the shortlist on.

questions.explanation: This test is a fair one: small, scoped, described in advance and the same for everybody. What is being sampled is the work he produces in the time he was given, which is also what the job will ask of him. An afternoon of polish tells them nothing about that, and it quietly promises a standard he cannot repeat once real deadlines arrive. Cutting three versions down to one fixes the wrong part of the plan, because the afternoon is still in it, and polish nobody asked for is not a better impression of him. Refusing on principle throws away a reasonable ask and a real chance. The option about secret timing is a guess about the agency's motives dressed up as insight. Work to the brief Dexter was actually given, and ask before starting if the brief is unclear.

questions.prompt: Rowel passed a GN Academy final exam last month, so he now has a credential code and a public verification page that anybody can open without an account. He is deciding how to put it on his resume for an operations role. Which version does the most for him?

options.text: A line naming the certification, who issued it, the fact that it was passed by exam, and the code a reader can check on the public page.
The word Certified placed in front of his job title at the top, so the first thing anybody sees is that he is qualified for this role.
A sentence saying the credential puts him above applicants without one, sitting next to the salary figure he has written into the document.
The credential badge printed large across the header, which a reader moving quickly will notice long before they reach a line of small text.

questions.explanation: A certificate is worth what the reader can check. Naming the issuer, what it required and the code that opens a public verification page turns it from a claim into evidence, and it costs one line. Certified in front of a job title is the common version and it is a quiet inflation of a title he does not hold, which is the same family of problem as a stretched date. Claiming the credential ranks him above other applicants asserts something he cannot know, and parking it beside a salary figure implies a credential entitles somebody to a rate, which it does not. A large badge is decoration standing where the evidence should be. None of them replace finished work: a credential opens the file, the portfolio keeps it open.

questions.prompt: Kris is interviewing for a salaried role at a Quezon City company and is asked what she expects to be paid. She is also holding an offer for an overseas remote contract that pays more per hour once she converts it, and she is about to name that converted figure. What should she do instead?

options.text: Name the converted figure and mention the other offer, since a competing offer in hand is the strongest basis any candidate can point to.
Say she will take whatever they offer, since staying flexible about pay is what keeps her inside a process she genuinely wants to be in.
Give a range for salaried roles of this kind here, and the basis for it, because the contract and the salary are not the same package.
Ask them to name a figure first and give no range at all, since whoever says a number first gives up ground in a negotiation like this.

questions.explanation: A salary and a contract rate are different arrangements, not two prices for one thing. The salaried package is administered by the employer and carries benefits, leave and contributions inside it. The contract rate is the whole of what she gets, and everything else is hers to carry. Converting one into the other and quoting it compares two things that were never comparable, and the interviewer hears a number with no basis under it. Waving the other offer looks like leverage and mostly reads as somebody who will leave. Saying she will take whatever they offer sets the floor at whatever they were hoping to pay. Refusing to give a range is the tactic people repeat to each other, and it hands the interviewer nothing to work with while she still has a role to fill.

questions.prompt: Two weeks after a final interview, Angel gets a two line rejection email. She has heard nothing at all on three other applications she sent that same month. What is the sensible next move?

options.text: A reply asking what she did wrong and what to fix, and another message if no answer comes, since feedback is what improves the next one.
One short reply thanking them and asking to be kept in mind for the next opening, then a single follow up on each of the other three.
Nothing at all, since a reply changes no decision that has been made and the other three have already answered her by staying silent.
A message to the other three saying she was turned down elsewhere and is free to start immediately, which shows them she is available now.

questions.explanation: A short reply to a rejection costs nothing and occasionally returns something, because the person they hired does not always stay and the next opening lands on the same desk. Meanwhile the other three are still live, and each is owed one follow up rather than a campaign. Asking what she did wrong feels like growth, and it asks a stranger to put a judgement about her in writing, which is more than a rejection email owes her, and chasing it turns a good impression into an awkward one. Doing nothing is the common choice and it closes a door that was still ajar. Announcing the rejection to the other three tells them somebody else assessed her and said no, which is not the thing she wants leading.

questions.prompt: An employer phones Nadine eleven days after she applied and asks whether she is still interested and whether she sent the sample they requested. She has applied to about twenty places this month and cannot remember which posting this is or what she sent them. What should she do?

options.text: Say yes to both questions and work out afterwards which role it was, since hesitating on a phone call loses the opportunity outright.
Apply to far fewer places from now on, because twenty is more than anybody can hold in their head and the memory is the real problem here.
Ask which role it is, say she will confirm within the hour, and then start one file logging what she sent, when, and what is due next.
Search her sent mail during the call and read the posting back to them, since the record already exists and needs no separate tracker.

questions.explanation: A search runs for weeks and memory does not, so the fix is a file: what she sent, to whom, when, and the next thing due. Asking which role it is costs nothing and beats a confident yes to a question she cannot answer, which is a promise she may already have broken. Cutting back to a handful of applications treats the symptom by shrinking the search itself. Digging through sent mail during the call feels resourceful, and an inbox is a pile rather than a record: it holds what she sent and never what is due next. That same file is where new evidence goes as well, because every application and every test task produces something for the inventory.
